newsitem.title: USA: Toy Tips analyzes toys without fear or favor.
newsitem.headline: Toy Tips analyzes toys without fear or favor.

text.p: "Children do not need a bazillion toys in the bedroom."
Marianne Szymanski's advice may fly in the face of the Saturday morning advertisers, who preach that more is better and the newest is the best.

But the market researcher and toy expert believes that a plaything is a child's learning tool, and like the proper hammer or screwdriver it needs to be thoughtfully chosen. It also has to have staying power and be appropriate for the child's age and play patterns. Toys are some of the most important tools for development of a child's personality and intellect, she says.

Szymanski, president of Toy Tips Inc., a Milwaukee-based research and marketing firm, has tested over 10,000 toys since 1991. Working with Marquette University researchers and an advisory team of over 50 educators, she has what she calls an unbiased view of the toy world and has come up with some suggestions for today's parents.
"A lot of toys are well made," she said, "however they (adults) need to take time and check them out... Some are copies of everything else."
Standards such as K-Nex and Erector sets are great toys in general, she said, but so much out there is is "junk. Some toys don't work."

Many toy manufacturers are playing off children's natural inclinations "to want something right away." But many of the toys advertised on Saturday morning television have no staying power. They are fun for a few minutes and then are relegated to the "bazillions" of unused toys in the bedroom.
Toys need to address where a child is in life, Szymanski said.
"You need to watch kids, especially at ages four to five, because they are developing and need tools to go to the next level."

First of all, toys have to be fun. That's why, she said, many of the classic toys, such Lego blocks, Colourforms or the game Clue, have such staying power. "The manufacturers did a great job in terms of development," she said.

The best toys are not necessarily the newest or the most expensive. They aid children in four major areas: personality development, intellectual development, social development and physical development.

Szymanski breaks down toy recommendations into these categories in the new booklet, "Toy Tips," just published by Toy Tips Inc. The toys included were culled from the thousands tested at some 50 sites nationwide over the past five years and represent 52 manufacturers.
Research on the toys was part of Szymanski's work for various clients, including battery companies, candy companies and fast food companies.
"We don't get paid by toy companies, which makes us different from other (research) firms. We do real research, with real children and psychologists," she said.
In "Toy Tips," sample toys are outlined for each developmental category.

Recommended toys that help with personality development help enhance a child's self confidence and make a child proud of his accomplishments. Examples include Little Tikes garden tool set (ages three to five); Playskool Soft Stuff Mr. Potato Head (ages three to seven); and Binney & Smith No-spill paints (ages four to 10).

Toys that aid intellectual development include those that promote open-ended play and allow a child to think independently. Examples include Fisher-Price Great Adventures castle (ages three to seven); Kenner EZ Bake oven (ages eight to 12); and Uncle Milton's Ant Farm (ages eight to adult).

Toys that benefit social development involve all family members and stress the importance of playing with others. Toys in this category include Milton-Bradley Chicken Limbo (ages four to eight); Oddzon Koosh Lawn Darts (ages five to 12); and Tyco Dr. Dreadful Creepy Clinic Set and Monster Medical Centre Set (ages six to 11).
Physical development can be enhanced by toys that encourage movement and stimulate the senses.

Some of these toys include Flexible Flyer Having a Ball (ages two to five); Parker Brothers Throw 'n Go Jenga (ages eight to adult); Tiger Electronics Brain Warp (ages eight to adult); and Berk Winnie the Pooh Learning The Shapes Foam Puzzle Mats (ages three to five).

Szymanski also has some toy tips for big kids. Toy Tips, which conducts an annual "executive toy test" for toys to alleviate corporate stress, notes the following: Cap Toys Stretch Armstrong, Ohio Art Etch-a-Sketch and Play Doh keychain.

For big kids -- aka adults -- toys should be small enough to fit in a briefcase, should not make more noise than a copying machine and should promote interaction with others while not distracting co-workers.

"Toy Tips" magazine will be published twice a year. The first issue is currently available for free at Toys 'r Us stores.
